title: Acute Delirium: Recognition, Reversible Causes and Emergency Escalation

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults aged 18 and over with suspected acute delirium in the emergency department (ED) or acute medical ward: recognition with the 4 As Test (4AT), search for and treatment of reversible causes, non-drug care, short-term drug treatment for severe distress, and when to escalate to a geriatrician, liaison psychiatrist or intensive care unit (ICU). Uses NICE CG103 (2023 update), SIGN 157 (2019) and the 4AT accuracy study, with US product labels for each medicine. Not for delirium caused by alcohol or sedative withdrawal (see the alcohol withdrawal topic), delirium in the ICU (use CAM-ICU or ICDSC), children, or palliative care of dying adults.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi national delirium guideline was found; the pathway follows NICE CG103 and SIGN 157, written for the United Kingdom and Scotland.

NICE CG103 gives no haloperidol dose. Doses (haloperidol 0.5 to 1 mg orally, maximum 2 mg in 24 hours; 0.5 mg intramuscularly, maximum 2 mg in 24 hours; risperidone 0.25 mg daily, maximum 1 mg in 24 hours; lorazepam 0.5 to 1 mg orally, maximum 2 mg in 24 hours; midazolam 2.5 mg intramuscularly, maximum 7.5 mg in 24 hours) come from the Scottish Delirium Association pathway in SIGN 157 Annex 4, which is expert consensus, not trial evidence. SIGN 157 Section 7.5 states the evidence is insufficient for a drug recommendation.
US product labels were read for contraindications and cautions. Haloperidol, risperidone, lorazepam and midazolam are not licensed for delirium in the US labels, so every delirium use is off-label.

The 4AT scoring threshold (score of 4 or more means possible delirium) comes from the 4AT accuracy study; the 4AT test sheet itself could not be opened (website blocked), so item scoring is quoted from the paper.
Typical adult reference ranges for blood tests are not taken from the guidelines; laboratories differ.

Haloperidol is contraindicated with other QTc-prolonging drugs (SIGN 157 Section 7.1); the US label gives 500 ms as the QTc above which torsades de pointes risk rises. A ECG threshold for withholding haloperidol was not set by NICE or SIGN.
The exact oral and intramuscular haloperidol maximum for patients over 80 years or with liver disease was not found beyond the label advice to use lower doses.

pathophysiology.summary: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness with an added disturbance of cognition, developing over hours to days and fluctuating (SIGN 157, Section 2). It is usually caused by one or more acute precipitants, such as infection, hypoxia, dehydration, pain, urinary retention, constipation or medicines, acting on a vulnerable brain (NICE CG103, Section 1.7.1; SIGN 157, Annex 4). Dementia, age 65 years or more, hip fracture and severe illness raise the risk (NICE CG103, Section 1.2.1). Opioids, benzodiazepines and anticholinergic drugs are common drug triggers; benzodiazepines markedly raise the odds of delirium (SIGN 157, Section 5). In up to 30% of cases no cause is found (SIGN 157, Annex 4).

symptoms: Recent change or fluctuation in thinking, such as poor concentration, slow responses or confusion (NICE CG103, Section 1.3.1).
Hallucinations, either visual or auditory (NICE CG103, Section 1.3.1).
Restlessness, agitation, reduced movement, poor appetite or disturbed sleep (NICE CG103, Section 1.3.1).
Withdrawal, difficulty following requests, or a change in mood or attitude (NICE CG103, Section 1.3.1).
physicalSigns: Reduced alertness or drowsiness, or marked agitation, on assessment of arousal (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Inattention: cannot say the months of the year backwards (4AT item 3) (4AT diagnostic accuracy study, Section Background).
Fluctuation over the day or an acute change from usual baseline reported by a relative or carer (NICE CG103, Section 1.3.1).
Signs of a cause: fever, hypoxia, dehydration, a full bladder, faecal loading, focal neurological signs (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
redFlags: Distress or behaviour that threatens the patient or others: try verbal and non-verbal de-escalation first, then consider drug treatment (NICE CG103, Section 1.7.3 and Section 1.7.4).
Hypoactive delirium (withdrawal, slow responses, reduced movement) is often missed: use the 4AT (NICE CG103, Section 1.3.2).
Possible serious cause: sepsis, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia or medicine intoxication needs action first (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
CT brain urgently if anticoagulated, head injury, focal neurological signs or persistent symptoms (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies: antipsychotics can cause severe reactions (NICE CG103, Section 1.7.4; Haloperidol injection label, Section Contraindications).
Delirium not resolving after one week or severe delirium: refer to the local specialist (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
precipitants: Infection or sepsis, urinary retention, constipation, hypotension, pain, dehydration, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia (SIGN 157, Annex 4).

Recent start, stop or dose change of opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, antispasmodics, antiepileptics, antihistamines, antihypertensives, steroids, tricyclic antidepressants, digoxin or antiparkinson drugs (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Age 65 years or more, cognitive impairment or dementia, hip fracture, severe illness (NICE CG103, Section 1.2.1).
Catheterisation, restraint, sensory impairment, recent surgery (SIGN 157, Annex 4).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Slow decline over months with stable alertness and no marked fluctuation; if delirium and dementia cannot be separated, manage as delirium first (NICE CG103, Section 1.6.3).
Acute worsening from the usual baseline, reported by an informant, with fluctuating attention (NICE CG103, Section 1.6.3).
Attention and orientation are usually preserved and onset is not hours to days; a formal assessment is needed because 4AT can be negative in delirium (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Recent heavy drinking or sedative stop with tremor and sweating; use the alcohol withdrawal pathway, not this one (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Focal neurological signs, head injury or anticoagulation: image the brain urgently (SIGN 157, Annex 4).

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Delirium screen: alertness, orientation, attention, acute change
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Takes about 2 minutes and needs no training; the screen is positive at 4 or more, then a clinician confirms the diagnosis (NICE CG103, Section 1.6.1; 4AT diagnostic accuracy study, Section Methods).

clinicalManagement.title: Act on life-threatening causes
actions: Check airway, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, pulse, temperature and capillary glucose (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Treat sepsis, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia or medicine intoxication straight away (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Assess with the 4AT and record the result (NICE CG103, Section 1.6.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Find and treat reversible causes
actions: Take an informant history for baseline cognition, alcohol intake and recent medicine changes (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Examine for infection, urinary retention, faecal loading and pain, and review every medicine started or stopped recently (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Send blood tests, urine and imaging as in Investigations; keep oxygen saturation above 95% except in type 2 respiratory failure (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Stop or reduce deliriogenic drugs, avoiding abrupt withdrawal of drugs with dependence (SIGN 157, Annex 4).

clinicalManagement.title: Give non-drug care
actions: Reorient and reassure the patient, explaining where they are and who you are; involve family (NICE CG103, Section 1.7.2).
Make sure glasses and hearing aids are in use, fluids and food are taken, sleep is protected, and avoid bed moves and unnecessary catheterisation (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Allow mobility within a safe area and relax visiting times (SIGN 157, Annex 4).

clinicalManagement.title: Manage severe distress or risk to others
actions: Use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation first (NICE CG103, Section 1.7.3).

Only if that fails and the patient is a risk to self or others, give one drug at the lowest dose, starting low (see medicines) and review every 24 hours (NICE CG103, Section 1.7.4; SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Check the QTc on an electrocardiogram (ECG) before haloperidol and do not combine it with other QTc-prolonging drugs (SIGN 157, Section 7.1).
Do not use antipsychotics if there are signs of parkinsonism or Lewy body dementia (SIGN 157, Annex 4).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate
actions: Refer to liaison psychiatry for severe agitation not responding to standard measures, doubt about the diagnosis, or if detention is being considered (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Refer to the local specialist after one week or if delirium is severe (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Arrange CT brain urgently for anticoagulation, head injury, focal neurological signs or persistent symptoms (SIGN 157, Annex 4).

clinicalManagement.title: Review and plan disposition
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Daily until two successive negative screens
actions: Repeat delirium screening until two successive daily screens are negative; reduce and stop antipsychotic as soon as the patient improves (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Repeat a cognitive assessment before discharge; if delirium does not resolve, re-evaluate causes and assess for dementia (NICE CG103, Section 1.7.5).
Document the diagnosis in hospital and primary care records and give information to the patient and family (NICE CG103, Section 1.6.4 and Section 1.8.1).

regimens.indication: Short-term control of severe distress in delirium
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with delirium and severe distress, can take oral medicine
regimens.dose: 0.5 mg to 1 mg orally as a single dose; maximum 2 mg in 24 hours (SIGN 157, Annex 4). Tablets are supplied as 0.5 mg and 1 mg (Haloperidol tablets label, Section How Supplied). Preparation: none; swallow whole.
regimens.frequency: Single doses as needed, reviewed every 24 hours; no more than 2 mg in any 24 hours
regimens.duration: Shortest possible, usually 1 week or less; stop as soon as the patient improves (NICE CG103, Section 1.7.4; SIGN 157, Section 7.1)
adjustments: Use the lowest dose in older, frail or debilitated patients; the label advises lower doses and more gradual titration in geriatric patients (Haloperidol injection label, Section Dosage and Administration).
Contraindicated with other QTc-prolonging drugs; combining makes use unlicensed (SIGN 157, Section 7.1).
Do not give if signs of parkinsonism or Lewy body dementia (SIGN 157, Annex 4).
Hepatic or renal impairment: no dose figure in the sources read; use the lowest dose and review (Haloperidol tablets label, Section Dosage and Administration).

teaching.scope: Adults aged 18 and over with suspected acute delirium in the emergency department (ED) or acute medical ward: recognition with the 4 As Test (4AT), search for and treatment of reversible causes, non-drug care, short-term drug treatment for severe distress, and when to escalate to a geriatrician, liaison psychiatrist or intensive care unit (ICU). Uses NICE CG103 (2023 update), SIGN 157 (2019) and the 4AT accuracy study, with US product labels for each medicine. Not for delirium caused by alcohol or sedative withdrawal (see the alcohol withdrawal topic), delirium in the ICU (use CAM-ICU or ICDSC), children, or palliative care of dying adults.
learningObjectives: Recognise delirium with the 4AT; hypoactive delirium is easy to miss.
Treat the cause first: sepsis, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, drugs, retention and constipation.
Use non-drug care and verbal de-escalation before any drug.
If a drug is needed use one drug, the lowest dose, and review daily.
pitfalls: Sedating the patient and not looking for a cause.
Giving haloperidol with another QTc-prolonging drug.
Giving regular instead of as-needed doses.
keyPoints: Delirium is a medical emergency, not a normal part of ageing.
A negative 4AT does not exclude delirium.
Antipsychotics are off-label and can harm in Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia.

patientEducation: Delirium is a sudden change in thinking that is common and usually temporary.
Please tell the team about any sudden change or fluctuation in behaviour.
Bring glasses, hearing aids and a list of medicines.
Recovery can take days to weeks; tell us if you or your relative is distressed by memories afterwards.
lifestyleAndDiet: Keep day and night routines and avoid unnecessary night-time procedures.
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician; geriatrician; liaison psychiatrist; pharmacist for medicine review; nursing team; occupational therapist and physiotherapist; family and carers.
dischargeCriteria: 4AT negative on two successive days; cause identified and treated; antipsychotic stopped or a clear plan for review; cognitive baseline recorded; carers informed; follow-up arranged for dementia assessment if delirium persisted.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Daily delirium screen until two successive negatives; repeat cognitive assessment before discharge; if symptoms persist beyond one week refer to a geriatrician or psychiatrist; primary care follow-up for dementia assessment (NICE CG103, Section 1.7.5; SIGN 157, Annex 4).
